Title: Horace Burgess’ Treehouse
Chunks: 0,1,2
Horace Burgess, a local minister and landscape architect in Crossville, constructed a small treehouse for his son, Kevin, in 1986. [9](https://abandonedonline.net/location/horace-burgess-treehouse/#cit9) The hideaway soon grew into a four-level, six-room home encompassing 2,300 square-feet, towering 50-feet above the ground and supported by two white oak trees and a few pines. The project cost about $3,000, with most of the wood coming from scraps from construction sites where he worked at and from neighbors.
The inspiration to build a more massive treehouse came to Burgess as he laid in bed in 1993. 2 11 Burgess, who had been going through a rough patch in life, stated that God had shown him the plans of the treehouse, which included art on the wall and an elevator.
> “If you build a tree house, I’ll see that you never run out of material.” [1](https://abandonedonline.net/location/horace-burgess-treehouse/#cit1)
Over the period of twelve years, Burgess erected a 97-foot-tall treehouse. 3 11 It was supported by an 80-foot-tall white oak tree and 15 other trees, 258,000 nails driven by a nail gun, and 500 penny nails driven by hand. [2](https://abandonedonline.net/location/horace-burgess-treehouse/#cit2) A belfry contained ten bells that were crafted out of ten oxygen-acetylene canisters weighing 5,700 pounds. [11](https://abandonedonline.net/location/horace-burgess-treehouse/#cit11) The treehouse doubled as a church where Burgess officiated 23 weddings. [2](https://abandonedonline.net/location/horace-burgess-treehouse/#cit2) When not used for service, the sanctuary doubled as a basketball court. 4 11

Because of its unique construction and its unofficial status as the world’s largest treehouse, Burgess’ wooden contraption became a tourist attraction [5](https://abandonedonline.net/location/horace-burgess-treehouse/#cit5) attracting up to 1,000 visitors per week. [10](https://abandonedonline.net/location/horace-burgess-treehouse/#cit10)
> “You’re above all your situations, circumstances, for a moment. Your eyes can see over all the stuff that’s under you.”  
>   
> – Horace Burgess [2](https://abandonedonline.net/location/horace-burgess-treehouse/#cit2)
On August 7, 2012, a state fire marshal performed an inspection on Burgess’ treehouse and ordered it closed as a safety precaution at the end of the month. [10](https://abandonedonline.net/location/horace-burgess-treehouse/#cit10) The state noted that it was 60 feet over code, did not have a fire alarm or sprinkler system and was not designed by a licensed architect. 2 6 7 10
In March 2018, the treehouse and its accompanying 139 acres of land were put up for sale with an asking price of $1.5 million. [12](https://abandonedonline.net/location/horace-burgess-treehouse/#cit12)On October 22, 2019, the treehouse and its supporting trees were burned to the ground with no cause determined. 7 8 Because of the all-wood construction, the inferno lasted just 15 minutes.

**Crossville** is a city in and the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Cumberland County, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_County,_Tennessee "Cumberland County, Tennessee"), United States.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-GR6-8) It is part of the [Crossville Micropolitan Statistical Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville_Micropolitan_Statistical_Area?action=edit&redlink=1 "Crossville Micropolitan Statistical Area (page does not exist)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-9) The population was 12,071 at the 2020 census.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-Census_2010-10)
Crossville developed at the intersection of a branch of the [Great Stage Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Stage_Road "Great Stage Road"), which connected the [Knoxville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knoxville,_Tennessee "Knoxville, Tennessee") area with the [Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee") area, and the [Kentucky Stock Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Stock_Road?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kentucky Stock Road (page does not exist)"), a cattle drovers' path connecting [Middle Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Tennessee "Middle Tennessee") with [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky") and later extending south to [Chattanooga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattanooga,_Tennessee "Chattanooga, Tennessee"). These two roads are roughly paralleled by modern US-40 and US-127, respectively.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-12)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/The_Palace_Theater.jpg/250px-The_Palace_Theater.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Palace_Theater.jpg)
Palace Theatre
[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Crossville_Tennessee_Highway_Patrol_Building.jpg/250px-Crossville_Tennessee_Highway_Patrol_Building.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crossville_Tennessee_Highway_Patrol_Building.jpg)
Native Stone Museum, one of many buildings in Crossville built of Crab Orchard Stone

*   [Cumberland Mountain State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_Mountain_State_Park "Cumberland Mountain State Park") is immediately south of Crossville.  
*   The [Cumberland Homesteads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_Homesteads "Cumberland Homesteads") are also south of Crossville.  
*   The Native Stone Museum, in a 1930s-era Tennessee Highway Patrol station on the courthouse square, is dedicated to Crab Orchard Stone, a local building material used in many of the city's buildings.  
*   The Eco Travel Plaza truck stop in Crossville has obtained notoriety on social media as "Celina 52 Truck Stop".  
*   The [Palace Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_Theater_(Crossville,_Tennessee) "Palace Theater (Crossville, Tennessee)"), which opened in 1938, still serves as a theater, performance venue, and meeting hall.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-23)  
*   The [United States Chess Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Chess_Federation "United States Chess Federation") moved its corporate offices to Crossville from [New Windsor, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Windsor,_New_York "New Windsor, New York"), in 2005. In 2022 the USCF announced that it would leave Crossville for St. Louis.  
*   The [Highway 127 Corridor Sale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highway_127_Corridor_Sale "Highway 127 Corridor Sale"), promoted as the world's largest [yard sale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yard_sale "Yard sale"), is held annually in August.  
*   The Cumberland County Playhouse is rural Tennessee's only major nonprofit professional performing arts resource, and one of rural America's 10 largest professional theaters. It serves more than 165,000 visitors annually with two indoor and two outdoor stages, young audience productions, a comprehensive dance program, a concert series and touring shows.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-24)  

*   Crossville calls itself "the golf capital of Tennessee" and features 12 courses: Stonehenge, Heatherhurst Crag, Heatherhurst Brae, Deer Creek, River Run, Four Seasons, The Bear Trace, Dorchester, Mountain Ridge, Renegade, Druid Hills, and Lake Tansi.  
*   The Cumberland County Fair is held every August.  
*   [Art Circle Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Circle_Public_Library "Art Circle Public Library")  
*   [Horace Burgess's Treehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse "Horace Burgess's Treehouse"), a treehouse and church, closed in 2012.  
*   A [free-speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-speech "Free-speech") zone on the Cumberland County Courthouse lawn was the site of several unofficial displays, including a statue of the [Flying Spaghetti Monster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Spaghetti_Monster "Flying Spaghetti Monster"), an Iraq and Afghanistan Soldier's Memorial, a miniature [Statue of Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Liberty "Statue of Liberty"), [chainsaw carvings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chainsaw_carving "Chainsaw carving") of a [nativity scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativity_scene "Nativity scene"), Jesus carrying the cross, and monkeys and bears.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-25) As of April 30, 2008, the lawn is no longer a free-speech zone due largely to the controversy caused by the Flying Spaghetti Monster statue.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-26)

*   [Mandy Barnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandy_Barnett "Mandy Barnett"), country music singer and actress born in Crossville[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-27)  
*   [Julie Ann Emery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Ann_Emery "Julie Ann Emery"), actress born and raised here[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-28)  
*   [Stormi Henley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stormi_Henley "Stormi Henley"), Miss Tennessee Teen USA 2009, Miss Teen USA 2009[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-29)  
*   [Milo Lemert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milo_Lemert "Milo Lemert"), posthumous [Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Honor "Medal of Honor") recipient for action near [Bellicourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellicourt "Bellicourt"), France, during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and buried in Crossville City Cemetery  
*   [Earl Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Lloyd "Earl Lloyd"), first [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") to play in an [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA "NBA") basketball game  
*   [Thomas Shadden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Shadden "Thomas Shadden"), politician, member of the [Tennessee General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_General_Assembly "Tennessee General Assembly") and Crossville mayor

**Crossville** is a city in and the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Cumberland County, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_County,_Tennessee "Cumberland County, Tennessee"), United States.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-GR6-8) It is part of the [Crossville Micropolitan Statistical Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville_Micropolitan_Statistical_Area?action=edit&redlink=1 "Crossville Micropolitan Statistical Area (page does not exist)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-9) The population was 12,071 at the 2020 census.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-Census_2010-10)
Crossville developed at the intersection of a branch of the [Great Stage Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Stage_Road "Great Stage Road"), which connected the [Knoxville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knoxville,_Tennessee "Knoxville, Tennessee") area with the [Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee") area, and the [Kentucky Stock Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Stock_Road?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kentucky Stock Road (page does not exist)"), a cattle drovers' path connecting [Middle Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Tennessee "Middle Tennessee") with [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky") and later extending south to [Chattanooga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattanooga,_Tennessee "Chattanooga, Tennessee"). These two roads are roughly paralleled by modern US-40 and US-127, respectively.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee#cite_note-12)

*   The Native Stone Museum, in a 1930s-era Tennessee Highway Patrol station on the courthouse square, is dedicated to Crab Orchard Stone, a local building material used in many of the city's buildings.  
*   The Eco Travel Plaza truck stop in Crossville has obtained notoriety on social media as "Celina 52 Truck Stop".

**Horace Burgess's Treehouse** (also known as the **Minister's Treehouse**) was a [treehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treehouse "Treehouse") and church in [Crossville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee "Crossville, Tennessee"), United States. Construction began in 1993, mostly by Burgess, who says that, in a vision, God commanded him to build a treehouse. It became a popular local attraction and was unofficially called the largest tree house in the world.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-slate2013-1) It was closed by the state on August 30, 2012, for [fire code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_code "Fire code") violations.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-hazzard-2) On October 22, 2019, the tree house completely burned to the ground in less than 15 minutes under unknown circumstances.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-Jones-4)

## History and description
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Burgess%27s_Treehouse&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and description")]
[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Horace_Burgess_Treehouse_Aug._27%2C_2011.jpg/250px-Horace_Burgess_Treehouse_Aug._27%2C_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Horace_Burgess_Treehouse_Aug._27,_2011.jpg)
The exterior of the treehouse

## History and description
Horace Burgess, a local minister, was praying in 1993 when he said God told him, "If you build a tree house, I'll see that you never run out of material."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-slate2013-1) Inspired by the vision, Burgess began building the treehouse and continued working on it for the next 12 years.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) The 97-foot-tall (30 m) tree house and church was supported by a still-living 80 ft (24 m)[white oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_oak "White oak") tree with a 12 ft-diameter (3.7 m) base, and relied on six other oak trees for support.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-usa2007-5) He built it using 258,000 nails with a nailgun, and about 500 pounds of penny nails driven by hand.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) The treehouse was located on Beehive Lane in [Crossville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee "Crossville, Tennessee").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-6)

## History and description
Over time, Burgess' treehouse became a popular tourist attraction.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyd2012-7) Burgess officiated 23 weddings in the treehouse church,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) and when not in service, the sanctuary doubled as a basketball court.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-independent2009-8) Although there is no [Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records") category for largest treehouse, it was often referred to as the world's largest.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-hp2012-9)[Pete Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Nelson "Pete Nelson"), the host of _[Treehouse Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treehouse\_Masters "Treehouse Masters")_ on [Animal Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_Planet "Animal Planet"), who has written six books about treehouses and owns a business building them, said it was "by far" the largest in the world.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3)

## History and description
In August 2012, the structure was closed to public access by the state because it had become a public attraction but did not follow building and fire safety codes.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-10)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-hazzard-2) It was a "deathtrap", said one official, "it was very cool, but also very dangerous."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-Jones-4) The structure stood vacant and dilapidated for years, becoming a frequent target of vandalism.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-fire-11) On October 22, 2019, the treehouse and its supporting trees completely burned to the ground in an inferno lasting about 15 minutes.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-12) The fire department responded; however, by the time they arrived nothing was left to save.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-fire-11) "It was basically a pile of rubble when we pulled up. The fire was so intense we had to park 500 yards away", said an official.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-Jones-4) Fire officials said there was no electricity on site and no electric storms. The recent new owner of the treehouse, who had no insurance, declined to open an investigation.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) Burgess said most of the marriages he officiated there had not lasted, and that he was relieved after the fire; the treehouse had "always been a pain" he said.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3)

texts.0: **Horace Burgess's Treehouse** (also known as the **Minister's Treehouse**) was a [treehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treehouse "Treehouse") and church in [Crossville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee "Crossville, Tennessee"), United States. Construction began in 1993, mostly by Burgess, who says that, in a vision, God commanded him to build a treehouse. It became a popular local attraction and was unofficially called the largest tree house in the world.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-slate2013-1) It was closed by the state on August 30, 2012, for [fire code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_code "Fire code") violations.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-hazzard-2) On October 22, 2019, the tree house completely burned to the ground in less than 15 minutes under unknown circumstances.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-Jones-4)

## History and description
Horace Burgess, a local minister, was praying in 1993 when he said God told him, "If you build a tree house, I'll see that you never run out of material."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-slate2013-1) Inspired by the vision, Burgess began building the treehouse and continued working on it for the next 12 years.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) The 97-foot-tall (30 m) tree house and church was supported by a still-living 80 ft (24 m)[white oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_oak "White oak") tree with a 12 ft-diameter (3.7 m) base, and relied on six other oak trees for support.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-usa2007-5) He built it using 258,000 nails with a nailgun, and about 500 pounds of penny nails driven by hand.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) The treehouse was located on Beehive Lane in [Crossville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossville,_Tennessee "Crossville, Tennessee").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-6)

## History and description
Over time, Burgess' treehouse became a popular tourist attraction.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyd2012-7) Burgess officiated 23 weddings in the treehouse church,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) and when not in service, the sanctuary doubled as a basketball court.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-independent2009-8) Although there is no [Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records") category for largest treehouse, it was often referred to as the world's largest.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-hp2012-9)[Pete Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Nelson "Pete Nelson"), the host of _[Treehouse Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treehouse\_Masters "Treehouse Masters")_ on [Animal Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_Planet "Animal Planet"), who has written six books about treehouses and owns a business building them, said it was "by far" the largest in the world.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3)

## History and description
In August 2012, the structure was closed to public access by the state because it had become a public attraction but did not follow building and fire safety codes.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-10)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-hazzard-2) It was a "deathtrap", said one official, "it was very cool, but also very dangerous."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-Jones-4) The structure stood vacant and dilapidated for years, becoming a frequent target of vandalism.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-fire-11) On October 22, 2019, the treehouse and its supporting trees completely burned to the ground in an inferno lasting about 15 minutes.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-12) The fire department responded; however, by the time they arrived nothing was left to save.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-fire-11) "It was basically a pile of rubble when we pulled up. The fire was so intense we had to park 500 yards away", said an official.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-Jones-4) Fire officials said there was no electricity on site and no electric storms. The recent new owner of the treehouse, who had no insurance, declined to open an investigation.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3) Burgess said most of the marriages he officiated there had not lasted, and that he was relieved after the fire; the treehouse had "always been a pain" he said.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Burgess's_Treehouse#cite_note-nyt-3)
